_meta.name: Ownership Structures
_meta.note: Module 02. The user reads an ownership chart, reviews documents, requests what's missing, then designates the beneficial owners. Every percentage has been calculated and verified before writing — a module that teaches a wrong calculation is worse than no module at all.

primer.title: The threshold
primer.question: Is Anna a beneficial owner?
primer.explain: 30% is above the 25% threshold. This is the simplest case, and the only one where the answer can be read directly off the chart.
primer.principle: The AMLR threshold is 25% or more of the shares, voting rights or other ownership interest, direct or indirect (Art. 52(1)). A threshold isn't an absolute rule — it's the point beyond which closer scrutiny is required.

primer.title: Multiply along the chain
primer.question: What is Tom's indirect ownership in Vasco Trading?
primer.explain: 50% × 50% = 25%: right on the threshold, so Tom is a beneficial owner. Percentages are multiplied along the chain, not added, and not simply the lower of the two. This works because no company in the chain controls the next one (50% is not 50% plus one). When one does, Article 54 applies instead: see the Ownership lesson.
primer.principle: Each layer dilutes. Tom holds half of a company that holds half of the target, so his indirect stake is 25%. AMLR Art. 52(1): multiply along the chain and add the chains, unless Article 54 applies.

primer.title: Add up the paths
primer.question: Does Rita reach the 25% threshold?

options.label: No — 16% indirect is below the threshold

primer.explain: 15% direct, plus 40% × 40% = 16% indirect. Total 31%. Neither path crosses the threshold on its own, which is exactly what makes this case dangerous. (No company here controls the next one, so multiplying and adding is the right method.)
primer.principle: Paths are additive. A structure designed to evade detection spreads ownership across several branches, none of which exceeds the threshold on its own. Looking at branches one at a time is the single most common mistake.

primer.title: Control without ownership
primer.note: A shareholders' agreement gives Karel the right to appoint and remove three of the five directors, and a veto over any disposal of assets.
primer.question: Is Karel a beneficial owner?

options.label: Yes — he exercises control by other means

primer.explain: Percentage ownership is only one of two tests. Appointing a majority of the board and holding a veto over disposals is control by other means within the meaning of Articles 51 and 53, regardless of shareholding.
primer.principle: Two paths lead to beneficial owner status: ownership and control. An analysis that only looks at percentages consistently misses the second one — and that's the one used to hide behind.

cases.title: A holding company and two partners
cases.subject: Kortrijk Textiles NV · corporate client · 25% threshold
cases.brief: An operating company held by a holding company, itself split between two partners. Nothing is hidden. The question is who counts, and the obvious arithmetic gives the wrong answer for one of them.

documents.name: Shareholder register — Kortrijk Textiles
documents.body: KT Holding BV: 80% of shares. Inès Lambert: 20% of shares. Register kept up to date, last entry March 2026.

documents.name: KvK extract — KT Holding BV
documents.body: Shares: Mina Vanhoutte 70%, Bram Vanhoutte 30%. Both are directors. No shareholders' agreement on file.

cases.why: KT Holding owns 80% of Kortrijk Textiles, so it controls it (50% plus one, Art. 53(2)(c)). When a company in the chain controls the next one, Article 54 applies instead of multiplying: the natural persons with an ownership interest of 25% or more in the controlling company are beneficial owners. Mina (70%) and Bram (30%) both qualify. Inès tops out at 20% direct, with no control.
cases.trap: Bram is the trap. Multiplying gives 80% × 30% = 24%, one point short, and the temptation is to stop there. But the multiplication rule applies 'unless Article 54 applies' (Art. 52(1)). Because the holding controls the client, Bram's 30% of the holding makes him a beneficial owner. A threshold is still a threshold: Inès, at 20% direct, is not one.
cases.law: AMLR Arts 51–54 — an ownership interest is 25% or more (Art. 52(1)); control through ownership is 50% plus one (Art. 53(2)(c)); where a company in the chain controls the next one, Art. 54 decides, not multiplication.
cases.lesson: Know when the arithmetic applies. Multiplying along the chain is the rule only where no company in the chain controls the next one; where one does, look at who holds 25% or more of the controlling company. Write the basis down in the file.

cases.title: Three branches, none decisive
cases.subject: Namur Logistique SA · corporate client · 25% threshold
cases.brief: Two holding companies and one direct stake. Taken alone, no branch crosses the threshold for one of the partners. Taken together, it's a different story.

documents.name: Shareholder register — Namur Logistique
documents.body: Ardenne Invest SPRL 50%, Sambre Participations 30%, Lena Gerard 15%, various minority holders 5%.

documents.name: CBE extract — Ardenne Invest SPRL
documents.body: Victor Gerard 50%, Lena Gerard 30%, various minority holders 20%. Victor is the managing director. No shareholders' agreement on file.

documents.name: RCS extract — Sambre Participations
documents.body: Dispersed shareholding. Lena Gerard is listed for 10%. No shareholder above 15%.

cases.why: No company in this structure controls the next one (none holds more than 50%), so indirect ownership is multiplied along each chain and the chains are added. Victor: 50% × 50% = 25%, right on the threshold. Lena accumulates three paths: 15% direct, 50% × 30% = 15%, and 30% × 10% = 3%. Total 33%. None of her three branches crosses the threshold on its own.
cases.trap: This is the case analysts miss most often. Working through the chart branch by branch, you see 15%, then 20% of one holding company, then 10% of another — three figures, all below the threshold, and it's easy to conclude too quickly. Aggregating by person, not by branch, is the only way to see Lena.
cases.law: AMLR Art. 52(1) — indirect ownership is calculated by multiplying along each chain and adding the chains together, unless Article 54 applies (a company in the chain controlling the next one).
cases.lesson: Spreading a stake across several vehicles, none of which crosses the threshold, is the simplest concealment technique there is, and it works against anyone reading a chart top to bottom. The countermeasure is methodological: calculate by person, not by branch.

cases.title: The holder isn't the beneficiary
cases.subject: Ostende Marine BV · corporate client · 25% threshold
cases.brief: The register shows a fiduciary company and a trust behind a 35% block. Look through both: for an express trust the law names a list of roles, not a percentage.

documents.name: Shareholder register — Ostende Marine
documents.body: Joris Maes 45%. Van Acker Family Trust, represented by Fiduciaire Delmas SA acting as trustee, 35%. Dispersed shareholding 20%.

documents.name: Fiduciary declaration
documents.body: Fiduciaire Delmas SA holds the shares as trustee of the Van Acker Family Trust. It holds no economic interest of its own and exercises no discretionary voting rights.

documents.name: Trust deed — Van Acker Family Trust
documents.body: Settlor: Marc Van Acker, born 1948, Belgian resident, father of the beneficiary. Trustee: Fiduciaire Delmas SA. Sole named beneficiary: Elin Van Acker, born 1974, Belgian resident. The trust is irrevocable. The trustee distributes income to the named beneficiary alone.

documents.name: Luxembourg register extract — Fiduciaire Delmas SA
documents.body: Sole shareholder: Paul Delmas, born 1969, Luxembourg resident, 100%. Paul Delmas is also the managing director.

cases.why: Joris holds 45% directly. The 35% block is held through an express trust, and for an express trust the law lists roles rather than a percentage: the settlor (Marc), the trustee, and the beneficiary (Elin). The trustee is a company, so the trust's beneficial owners also include the beneficial owner of that company (Paul, its sole shareholder). The fiduciary company itself is not a natural person and is not designated.
cases.trap: Three errors are waiting here. Naming the fiduciary company: it is the name in the register, and it is not a natural person. Stopping at Elin, because the deed names her as the only beneficiary and 35% belongs to her economically: the settlor and the trustee count too. Or forgetting that the trustee is itself a company, whose own beneficial owner must be found. All four documents needed reading, not just the register.
cases.law: AMLR Art. 58(1): the beneficial owners of an express trust are all of the settlors, trustees, protectors (if any), beneficiaries and anyone else exercising ultimate control; Art. 58(3): where one of those positions is held by a legal entity, the beneficial owners of that entity are included too; Art. 55: the beneficial owners of a legal arrangement holding an interest in a company are beneficial owners of that company; Art. 66: nominees must disclose who they act for. This fictional case has no protector.
cases.lesson: The shareholder register says who holds, not who benefits or who controls. A trust is a list of roles, and a corporate trustee has owners of its own. Request the deed and the trustee's register extract before you conclude.

cases.title: Eight percent and the board of directors
cases.subject: Liège Composites SA · corporate client · 25% threshold
cases.brief: The shareholding is fragmented: no one comes close to the threshold. The file therefore looks like it has no beneficial owner. This is exactly when you need to look beyond percentages.

documents.name: Shareholder register — Liège Composites
documents.body: Meuse Capital Fund 22%, Sofia Renard 14%, Karel Dumont 8%, dispersed shareholding 56% (no holder above 3%).

documents.name: Coordinated articles of association
documents.body: The board has five members. Asset disposal decisions above €500,000 require unanimous board approval.

documents.name: Shareholders' agreement dated 4 February 2025
documents.body: Karel Dumont holds the right to appoint and remove three of the five directors, and a veto over any disposal of assets, merger, or capital increase. This right is granted to him personally and is not tied to his shareholding.

cases.why: No natural person reaches 25% through ownership. But Karel appoints a majority of the board and holds a veto over structural decisions: that's control by other means, which makes him a beneficial owner regardless of his 8%.
cases.trap: If the agreement isn't requested, the file concludes with 'no beneficial owner at the threshold, senior managing official retained by default' — a perfectly reasoned and perfectly wrong conclusion. Falling back on the senior managing official is only legitimate once both routes, ownership and control, have been exhausted. Exhausting them means requesting the agreements.
cases.law: AMLR Arts 51 and 53(3) — control by other means; Art. 22(2) — recourse to senior managing officials applies only as a last resort, after all possible means of identification are exhausted.
cases.lesson: A fragmented shareholding isn't the absence of a beneficial owner — it's often a sign that control needs to be looked for elsewhere. Defaulting to the senior managing official is the most common way to close a file cleanly without having identified anything.

cases.title: The company that owns itself
cases.subject: Gand Maritime NV · corporate client · 25% threshold
cases.brief: A holding company owns the target, and the target owns a stake in the holding company. The calculation loops if you let it.

documents.name: Shareholder register — Gand Maritime
documents.body: Schelde Holding NV 60%, Omar Haddad 22%, Sara Willems 8%, various minority holders 10%.

documents.name: CBE extract — Schelde Holding NV
documents.body: Sara Willems 50%, Gand Maritime NV 20% (cross-shareholding), various minority holders 30%. The cross-shareholding dates from the 2022 restructuring.

cases.why: Schelde Holding owns 60% of Gand Maritime, so it controls it (50% plus one). Article 54 then applies: the natural persons with 25% or more of the controlling holding are beneficial owners, and Sara holds 50% of it (she also holds 8% directly). Omar stays at 22% direct, below the threshold. Gand Maritime's cross-shareholding in its own holding company doesn't propagate: it's logged as a loop and the traversal stops there.
cases.trap: Two ways to get this wrong. Running the loop and artificially inflating the percentages — the calculation converges mathematically but no longer describes anything real. Or treating the cross-shareholding as an additional shareholder and diluting the others. A cross-shareholding dilutes the real economic interest of external shareholders; it belongs in the file as a flag, not in the calculation.
cases.law: AMLR Art. 51 — beneficial owners are natural persons; Art. 54 — where a company in the chain controls the next one, the persons with an ownership interest in the controlling company are beneficial owners. A circular shareholding creates no additional beneficial owner.
cases.lesson: When a chain loops back to an entity already traversed, stop and note it. The fact is worth flagging — cross-shareholdings are also used to obscure real economic interest — but it isn't something you calculate.

cases.title: The file that can't be concluded
cases.subject: Anvers Commodities BVBA · corporate client · 25% threshold
cases.brief: The chart is complete, the documents are consistent, and the one thing that matters is missing.

documents.name: Shareholder register — Anvers Commodities
documents.body: Redstone Holdings Ltd 62%, Pieter Aerts 20%, various minority holders 18%.

documents.name: Certificate of incorporation — Redstone Holdings Ltd
documents.body: Incorporated in the Seychelles. Sole shareholder: Corporate Nominees Ltd, acting as nominee. Sole director provided by the same service provider. No public beneficial ownership register in this jurisdiction.

documents.name: Service provider declaration
documents.body: Corporate Nominees Ltd confirms it holds the shares on behalf of a beneficiary, without naming them. The provider states that disclosure is possible upon a formal, reasoned request to its compliance department.

requests.name: Search for a public register in the Seychelles
requests.empty: No public beneficial ownership register exists in this jurisdiction. The search returns nothing.

cases.why: Pieter tops out at 20%, below the threshold. The 62% block is held by a structure whose beneficial owner cannot be identified with the documents available. This isn't a partial conclusion — it's the impossibility of concluding, and Article 21 draws the consequences from that.
cases.trap: Three wrong outcomes, all superficially defensible. Naming Pieter because he's the only visible natural person. Naming the nominee because it's the one in the register. Or falling back to the senior managing official as a last resort — when that route assumes the other paths have been exhausted, and here they haven't: the provider explicitly opened a disclosure channel.
cases.law: AMLR Art. 22(2) — where, after exhausting all possible means, no beneficial owner is identified, record that and identify senior managing officials; Art. 21 — where due diligence measures cannot be completed, the relationship must not be established.
cases.lesson: Professional courage here means writing 'undetermined' rather than a plausible name. A file that names the wrong beneficial owner is worse than one that acknowledges the gap — the first looks complete and will never be reopened.
